- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward — reduce forecasted drop magnitude.
- After sharp price spikes, model often overshoots downward in subsequent days — cap forecast decline to match recent mean or add slight upward bias.
- If sentiment is positive and price is trending up, model frequently underestimates upside — increase forecast by 1–2% relative to recent mean.
- Model consistently underestimates true price in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) when sentiment is neutral or slightly negative — adjust downward bias by 0.5–1.5% for short-term forecasts.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed, model overfits to recent highs/lows — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ price + sentiment-weighted trend.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overestimates mean reversion — reduce forecast by 1–3% if sentiment is weak or neutral, especially if recent price is above 30-day average.
- If sentiment is consistently negative and price is falling, model tends to forecast a steeper decline — reduce forecast slope by 20–40% to avoid “panic” overreaction.
- Model underestimates true price when sentiment is positive but price is near support — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to avoid “bottoming too early.”
